summary: Describes an optional method for encoding explicit sensitivity labels on IPv6 packets. It is meant only for multi-level secure networks that are both trusted and trustworthy. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Government networks sometimes mark data as secret or public. This note describes a way to stamp each packet with such a label in specially protected networks.

subtitle: Labels for multi-level secure packet classification in closed IPv6 networks.

tldr.problem: Government and military networks need to mark packets with security sensitivity levels and compartments to enforce mandatory access controls. IPv4 had this capability for decades, but IPv6 lacked a standard way.
tldr.mechanism: CALIPSO adds an optional IPv6 hop-by-hop header containing a domain of interpretation, sensitivity level, and compartment bitmap. Routers and endpoints can read these labels and decide whether to forward or accept packets.
tldr.outcome: Networks for defense, government, and high-security enterprises can now mark and enforce access policies on IPv6 traffic, but only in closed, trusted networks.

today: RFC 5570 is an Informational RFC and has not been obsoleted. It is used in closed government, military, and enterprise MLS networks, particularly in NATO and US Department of Defense deployments. While the IESG notes that hop-by-hop options are problematic on the global Internet, they confirmed CALIPSO is appropriate for this limited, closed environment.

sections.title: Labels for Multi-Level Secure Networks
sections.content:
RFC 5570 defines CALIPSO (Common Architecture Label IPv6 Security Option), a method to encode sensitivity labels on IPv6 packets. The RFC is descended from earlier IPv4 labeling work, adapted for IPv6 and modern multi-level secure (MLS) environments.

Organizations like governments, militias, and secure enterprises have used IPv4 packet labels for about two decades to control access to classified or sensitive data. The need continues: some applications multiplex traffic at different sensitivity levels over a single connection, such as a distributed file system or voice protocol. Without per-packet labels, routers and endpoints cannot enforce mandatory access controls. CALIPSO provides this for IPv6 in closed, trusted networks only; the RFC warns that labeled packets must never appear on the public Internet.
sections.plainLanguage: A government network marks every packet with how secret it is, so routers know who is allowed to see it. CALIPSO is the way to do it.

sections.title: The Four Components of a Label
sections.content:
A CALIPSO sensitivity label has four parts. The Domain of Interpretation (DOI) is an opaque identifier pointing to a set of policies—for example, the US Department of Defense, a NATO coalition, or a corporation. It tells the network which rules apply to the label. The Sensitivity Level is an 8-bit number representing relative secrecy, from 0 (unclassified) to 255 (most secret). Levels have a strict ordering: if a user can read level 5, they can read levels below it.

The third component is the Compartment Set, a bitmap of up to 64 bits in the header. Each bit represents a compartment, category, or access program—for example, "Finance", "R&D", or "Nuclear". Unlike sensitivity levels, compartments do not imply access: access to one compartment does not grant access to another. The fourth component is Releasability, encoded as inverted compartment bits. A releasability like "ReleasableTo_UK" uses a zero bit to mean allowed and one to mean forbidden, opposite to compartments. The design ensures intermediate systems need not know whether a bit means compartment or releasability; they just compare labels using the same logic.
sections.plainLanguage: A label has four things: which country owns the rules, how secret it is, which teams can see it, and which countries it can be sent to. The network does not need to know what the bits mean.

sections.title: The CALIPSO Hop-by-Hop Option Header
sections.content:
CALIPSO is an IPv6 hop-by-hop option, visible to routers along the path so they can enforce access control, not a destination option. The header begins with two 8-bit fields: the option type (binary 00000111) and the option length in octets (minimum 8 when the compartment bitmap is absent). Next comes the 32-bit DOI field, followed by an 8-bit compartment length (in 32-bit words, minimum 0) and an 8-bit sensitivity level. A 16-bit CRC-16 checksum covers the entire option to protect against accidental corruption; implementations must compute it on transmission and verify on reception.

The variable-length compartment bitmap follows, padded as needed to align the option to 64 bits total. The overall design prioritizes simplicity so routers can implement access control in hardware. Complex formats like the earlier IPv4 Commercial IP Security Option (CIPSO) were difficult for routers to parse at wire speed.
sections.plainLanguage: The header is short and simple: which rules apply, a secret level number, a checksum, and a list of compartments. Routers can check it in a few clock cycles.

sections.title: How Endpoints and Routers Handle Labels
sections.content:
When a labeled IPv6 packet arrives at an end system (a host or router terminating the packet), the node must verify the CALIPSO checksum, confirm the DOI is known and permitted for the receiving interface, and check that the packet's sensitivity label falls within the allowed range for that interface. If all checks pass, the node converts the network label to its internal format and delivers the data to the application with label information. If any check fails—wrong checksum, unknown DOI, or out-of-range label—the packet is silently dropped and the event is logged as a security fault.

An intermediate system (a router forwarding the packet) performs the same input checks, then forwards based on the sensitivity label and the outgoing interface's constraints. The router may translate the label from one DOI to another if trusted to do so, or it may relabel the packet to match local policy. Connection-oriented protocols like TCP must maintain the same label for the entire session, but stateless protocols like UDP allow different labels on different packets.
sections.plainLanguage: When a packet arrives, the system checks the label is valid. If it is, the packet goes where the label says. If not, it is thrown away. Routers forward packets with the same label to all interfaces allowed for that label.

sections.title: Design and Deployment Considerations
sections.content:
CALIPSO is designed only for closed, physically and electronically isolated networks. The RFC warns of severe consequences if a labeled packet escapes to the public Internet, so deploying organizations must have strong incentive and control to prevent it. MLS networks typically operate in guarded buildings or with cleared personnel only; many do not use commercial firewalls or network address translation, avoiding complexity and potential bypasses. The option MUST NOT use the NULL DOI (all zeros) on the wire, and nodes MUST support at least two concurrent DOIs to allow smooth migration from one DOI to another without downtime.

The RFC builds on formal work by Bell and LaPadula, extending their mandatory access control model to include multiple DOIs, compartments, and releasability. It emphasizes that automatic label downgrading (reducing security classification) must not occur unless explicitly enabled by a system security officer. Upper-layer protocols face complexities: a TCP connection in an MLS system is identified not just by the 5-tuple of addresses and ports, but also by an internal sensitivity label, unlike single-level Internet TCP.
sections.plainLanguage: The labels only work in small, trusted networks where everyone knows each other. If one escapes to the Internet, secrets are lost. Labels never change automatically; a human must approve any reduction in security level.
